title: I thank my God (Philippians 1:1–11)
hookLine: Paul, in prison, thanks God every time he remembers them
last: THE WORLD COULD NOT CONTAIN IT.

lines: A PRISONER, NOT KNOWING HIS FATE.
cards: Next come three short letters, one after another: Philippians, James, and the first letter of John. Joy, faith and love. The first is a thank-you note written by a prisoner.
Paul is in chains. Scholars debate where: Rome, Ephesus, maybe Caesarea. He doesn't know if he'll be released or executed.
He writes to a small church in a Roman colony in northern Greece, a church that's been sending him money and help. A letter from prison might open with complaint, or fear, or a request.
Instead, the first thing Paul says is thank you.

teach.h: EVERY TIME THEY COME TO MIND: THANKS.
teach.b: In the King James Bible: "I thank my God upon every remembrance of you." Every time they come to mind, he gives thanks. Who are they?
In the book of Acts, Paul comes to Philippi after a vision of a man of Macedonia asking for help.

teach.h: LYDIA AND A JAILER: THE FIRST CHURCH.
teach.b: Lydia, a businesswoman who sold purple cloth, is baptized there with her household. Then a jailer, after an earthquake shakes open the prison doors one night.
A merchant and a prison guard, among the church's first members, and they've stuck with Paul ever since. He thanks them "For your fellowship in the gospel from the first day until now."

Fellowship is the Greek koinonia: partnership, sharing, a common life. Here it's practical. They shared his work, and later in the letter he thanks them for sending money more than once, when no other church did.
Then the confidence: "he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ." Paul doesn't say you'll finish what you started.

teach.h: GOD WILL FINISH WHAT HE BEGAN.
teach.b: He says God will finish what he started in you. Some readers hold onto that line in slow seasons, when they feel unfinished.
Then he prays for them: "that your love may abound yet more and more in knowledge and in all judgment." Not just more love: love that sees clearly, with good judgment.

teach.h: I THANK MY GOD UPON EVERY REMEMBRANCE OF YOU.
teach.b: One word keeps surfacing through this short letter: joy. Rejoice. From a prison cell.
That's the thread for the next few weeks.

how: Many Christians begin their prayers with thanksgiving for particular people, as Paul does, and some write Philippians 1:6 in cards for people starting something new or going through a slow season.

games.q: you're in chains, unsure if you'll live. you're writing to friends who've supported you. how do you open the letter?
o: tell them how hard prison is.
thank God every time you remember them.
ask them to send more money.
games.why: "I thank my God upon every remembrance of you." the first thing a prisoner writes is thanks.

practice: Let a face come to mind, someone who has been a partner to you in something good, a teacher, an old friend, a coworker who covered for you, someone who believed in you early, and remember what they actually did.
If you pray, thank God for them by name, the way Paul did; if not, simply hold them in thanks.

wordCard.voice: Koinonia. Greek for fellowship, partnership, sharing: Paul's word for the Philippians, who shared his work.
